description: Scandinavian kingdom (c. 936–present) that controlled the Sound between the North and Baltic Seas, giving it extraordinary leverage over Baltic trade; its eleventh-century North Sea empire under Cnut, its role in the Northern Crusades, and its Baltic commercial rivalries with the Hanseatic League made it the dominant Scandinavian power through most of the medieval period.

temporal.notes: Traditional founding under Harald Bluetooth; Christianization marker

lifecycle_phases.description: Harald Bluetooth (958–986) unifies Denmark and converts to Christianity; his runestone at Jelling records that he 'made the Danes Christian.' His son Sven Forkbeard conquers England (1013). Cnut the Great (1016–1035) rules a North Sea Empire comprising England, Denmark, Norway, and part of Sweden, the greatest Scandinavian empire. His sophisticated Christian kingship style transforms Scandinavian governance.

Valdemar I 'the Great' (1157–1182) reunifies Denmark after civil wars and begins Baltic expansion. Valdemar II 'the Victorious' (1202–1241) extends Danish control from Holstein to Estonia, creating a Baltic empire. After his defeat at the Battle of Bornhöved (1227), Denmark loses most German territories. The Black Death (1349–1350) severely reduces the population.

Valdemar IV 'Atterdag' (1340–1375) restores Danish power and sacks Visby (1361). His daughter Margaret I becomes Queen of Denmark, Norway, and Sweden through the Kalmar Union (1397), ruling the combined Scandinavian realm as the most powerful woman in medieval European history. Denmark dominates the union, controlling the Øresund strait and its toll revenues.

rise_factors.description: Denmark's control of the Øresund (Sound) strait, the only passage between the North Sea and Baltic Sea, gave it a permanent toll-collection chokepoint; every merchant ship trading with the Baltic had to pay Denmark, providing enormous revenues regardless of Danish military power

The Danish peninsula and islands commanded both the entrance to the Baltic and the Skagerrak/Kattegat passages; this central position in northern European maritime commerce was a structural geographic advantage that no other power could replicate

Control of the Øresund strait gave Denmark a choke-point on Baltic–North Sea trade. Tolls collected at Helsingør (Elsinore) after 1429 became a primary revenue source funding Danish military expansion.
Cnut the Great (r.1016–1035) assembled a maritime empire spanning England, Denmark, and Norway, demonstrating Danish capacity for large-scale naval power projection using royal fleet organization.
The establishment of the Archbishop of Lund (1103) made Denmark ecclesiastically independent from Hamburg-Bremen, boosting royal authority over church appointments and ecclesiastical revenues.

Margaret I's formation of the Kalmar Union (1397) united Denmark, Norway, and Sweden under Danish leadership, making Denmark the senior power of a Scandinavian bloc commanding both the Baltic and North Sea.

decline_factors.description: Danish noble power constrained royal authority; the Danehof (noble assembly) limited taxation and military levies, making it difficult to sustain the large-scale military campaigns needed to hold northern German territories

The Hanseatic League's economic power and the rising north German princes combined to force Denmark out of Holstein and Holstein at the Battle of Bornhöved (1227); the League repeatedly supported Danish nobles against the crown

The Hanseatic League systematically undercut Danish merchants, gained trade privileges through the Treaty of Stralsund (1370), and periodically blockaded Danish ports, constraining commercial sovereignty.
Repeated Swedish revolts (particularly under Engelbrekt Engelbrektsson, 1434–36 and Sten Sture the Elder) drained Danish military resources and foreshadowed the dissolution of the Kalmar Union.

sources.author: Sawyer, Birgit, and Sawyer, Peter
sources.title: Medieval Scandinavia: From Conversion to Reformation, circa 800–1500
